title: Light and maintain a fire
summary: Prepare all three sizes of fuel before striking the match.
steps: Choose a spot sheltered from the wind, clear the ground for 3 metres around, away from low branches.
Gather BEFORE lighting: tinder (very fine and dry: dry grass, birch bark, cotton), kindling (twigs the size of a pencil), and fuel (branches the size of your wrist).
Make a nest of tinder, then arrange the kindling as a teepee around it, leaving an opening facing the wind.
Light the tinder from below, blow gently at the base.
Gradually add larger and larger wood without smothering the flame.
warnings: Put it out completely with water and stir the ashes before leaving.
tips: Cotton soaked in petroleum jelly: an excellent fire starter that keeps for years in a small box.
Dead wood still attached to trees is drier than wood on the ground.

title: Keep the heat in a home without heating
summary: Power cut in winter: concentrate the heat instead of losing it.
steps: Gather in a single room, preferably small and not exposed.
Close doors, shutters and curtains; block the bottom of doors with towels.
Wear several layers of clothing, a hat and socks, and stay dry.
Sleep together in the same room, insulated from the floor by mattresses or blankets.
Eat hot meals regularly, have hot drinks.
warnings: Never a barbecue, brazier or generator indoors (carbon monoxide).
tips: A tent pitched inside the room holds body heat much better.
Hot-water bottle: a glass bottle filled with hot water, wrapped in cloth.

title: Cooking without electricity
summary: Safe ways to heat water and meals.
steps: Camping stove (gas, alcohol): only in a very well-ventilated place or outdoors.
Barbecue, wood fire: outdoors only.
Save fuel: lid on the pan, food cut small, quick-cooking dishes (thin pasta, couscous, oats).
Passive cooking: bring to the boil for a few minutes, then wrap the closed pan in blankets or a sleeping bag to finish cooking.
warnings: Never store gas canisters near a heat source.

title: Light a fire without a lighter or matches
summary: Fire steel, lens, battery: alternatives that really work.
materials: Fire steel, magnifying glass, or 9 V battery and steel wool
steps: Fire steel (ferrocerium): scrape the rod firmly with the back of a knife, right against the tinder; the very hot sparks ignite it.
Magnifying glass, reading-glasses lens, polished can bottom: focus the sun into a tiny point on dark, dry tinder.
Battery and fine steel wool: rub both terminals of a 9 V battery on the steel wool, which glows red; put it straight into the tinder.
In every case, prepare the tinder, kindling and fuel BEFORE trying.
tips: The friction method (bow drill) is very hard without practice: don't count on it in a real situation.
Slip a fire steel into every kit: it works even when wet.

title: Making fire in wet weather
summary: Finding dry wood in the rain.
steps: Look for dead branches still attached to trees, and the underside of fallen trunks.
Split the wood: the core stays dry even when the outside is wet.
Carve “feather sticks”: long, thin shavings left attached, which catch fire easily.
Build a platform of branches to keep the fire off the wet ground.
Dry the next wood near the fire.
